note: The rhyme patterns a lyric section can be written to, as data, so that a template can demand one and the checker can verify it. Patterns are written as letter strings over line positions: A, B, C mark distinct rhyme sounds and X marks a deliberately unrhymed line.
detectability_note: The checker's rhyme detection is spelling-based and approximate (see docs/design/tag-vocabulary.md 7.1). A missed rhyme may be the detector's fault rather than the writer's, so every result here is advisory and the `strictness` field says how much weight to give a mismatch.

schemes.name: Couplets
schemes.description: Lines 1-2 rhyme, then lines 3-4 rhyme. Two independent pairs.
schemes.notes: The most common scheme in modern popular lyric. Easy to write, easy to make monotonous: vary the pair sounds between sections.

schemes.name: Alternating
schemes.description: Lines 1 and 3 rhyme; lines 2 and 4 rhyme.
schemes.notes: Carries a section forward better than couplets because the rhyme resolves late. Harder to sustain over four lines without forcing.

schemes.name: Common metre / ballad
schemes.description: Only lines 2 and 4 rhyme. Lines 1 and 3 are free.
example: the diner on the corner shut its doors (A)
schemes.notes: The most forgiving useful scheme: half the lines are unconstrained, which suits narrative where forcing a rhyme would distort the story. A good default when the brief is content-led rather than hook-led.

schemes.name: Monorhyme
schemes.description: Every line rhymes with every other.
schemes.notes: Powerful and quickly tiring. Works best in short sections, or where the rhyme sound is chosen for its vowel colour rather than for the words it forces.

schemes.name: Enclosed
schemes.description: Lines 1 and 4 rhyme; the inner pair rhyme with each other.
example: I drive the long way home (A)
past the corner where we stand (B)
your voice still in my hand (B)
schemes.notes: Feels enclosed and deliberate. Rare in pop because the delayed resolution can read as fussy; very effective in a bridge.

schemes.name: Blues quatrain
schemes.description: The first line is repeated, then a rhyming punchline.
example: woke up this morning and the sky was grey (A)
woke up this morning and the sky was grey (A)
looked out my window, nothing went my way (A)
and I've got to get away (B)
schemes.notes: The repetition is structural, not a mistake: line 2 restates line 1 and line 3 turns it. Pairs with the twelve_bar_blues structure template.

schemes.name: AABA
schemes.description: Two rhyming lines, a contrasting line, then a return to the first rhyme.
schemes.notes: The rhyme sound returns after a detour, which gives the section a small arc. The basis of the 32-bar AABA form.

schemes.name: Sparse
example: a phone that will not glow (A)
schemes.notes: Leaves most lines unrhymed, so the ones that do rhyme land hard. Useful when the syllable count matters more than the rhyme.

schemes.name: Even lines only
schemes.description: Odd lines are explicitly unrhymed; even lines rhyme.
example: open up the canvas and the slate is blank (X)
drag another node into the light (A)
checkpoint loader first and then you set the rank (X)
and the queue is running right (A)
schemes.notes: Distinct from ABCB only in intent: X is a decision, not an accident. Useful for technical or narrative content where an odd-line rhyme would be forced.

schemes.name: Extended couplets
schemes.description: Couplets continued across eight lines, each pair with a new sound.
schemes.notes: Only for sections long enough to carry eight lines. Demands four distinct rhyme sounds, so it is prone to forced pairs near the end.

schemes.name: Chained
schemes.description: Each four-line block uses its own pair of rhymes, and blocks alternate to form an eight-line section.
schemes.notes: A common way to keep a long verse from settling. Treat each four-line block as its own scheme when checking.

schemes.name: Free verse
schemes.description: No rhyme required. Rhythm and imagery carry the section instead.
schemes.notes: A legitimate choice rather than an absence of one. In a template it means the rhyme check is skipped, not that it is expected to fail.

schemes.name: Internal rhyme
schemes.description: The rhyme falls inside the line as well as at the end; there may be no end rhyme at all.
example: I drive the lon- way home alon-
no li- no pho- just the road
cold ni-, old fli-, hold tight
schemes.notes: The dominant technique in modern rap. The end-rhyme detector cannot see it, so a template using this scheme should expect the rhyme check to report a mismatch rather than trusting it.
